stem: In the OWASP Mobile Top 10 2024, which risk absorbed the 2016 categories Code Tampering and Reverse Engineering?
explanation: 2016 M8 Code Tampering and M9 Reverse Engineering merged into 2024 M7 Insufficient Binary Protections.
optionNotes: M4 covers injection and unvalidated data.
M8 covers insecure settings such as debug flags and cleartext traffic.
M2 covers third-party components and the build pipeline.
Correct: binary attacks (reverse engineering and tampering) are now one category.

stem: A tester finds that a shopping app still connects to its API when the server presents a self-signed, expired certificate. Which OWASP Mobile 2024 risk is this?
explanation: OWASP M5 lists accepting self-signed, revoked, expired or wrong-host certificates as an attack vector. Validate certificates and consider pinning.
optionNotes: M1 is about how credentials are stored or used, not certificate validation.
M9 is about data at rest on the device.
Correct: accepting bad certificates breaks TLS protection in transit.
M7 is about reverse engineering and tampering with the binary.

stem: A popular analytics SDK bundled in a company's app is found to be quietly sending contact lists to an unknown server. Which OWASP Mobile 2024 risk does this illustrate?
explanation: M2 covers vulnerable or malicious third-party libraries and SDKs. Vet dependencies, keep an inventory and monitor their behavior.
optionNotes: Privacy is harmed, but the root cause the question describes is the untrusted third-party component.
Correct: the weakness came in with a third-party component.
No authentication or authorization flaw is described.
Nothing here is about weak cryptography.

stem: By changing `accountId=1001` to `accountId=1002` in a request sent by a banking app, a tester sees another customer's statements. Which risk is this?
explanation: OWASP M3 lists IDOR as a sign of missing authorization. The back end must check that the caller owns the object on every request.
optionNotes: Correct: an IDOR, a missing server-side authorization check.
The input is valid; the server simply never checks ownership.
The traffic may be encrypted; the flaw is in authorization.
It is a logic flaw in authorization, not a setting.

stem: A flashlight app asks for contacts, precise location and the microphone, and sends that data to an ad network. Which OWASP Mobile 2024 risk fits best?
explanation: OWASP M6 recommends minimizing the amount and variety of personal data an app processes; data it never collects cannot leak.
optionNotes: Nothing about reverse engineering or tampering.
No input handling flaw is described.
Correct: it collects and shares personal data it does not need.
Nothing about cryptography.

stem: During testing, the device log shows `I/LoginActivity: user=ana@corp.com token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...`. What is the problem and the fix?
options: Sensitive data is written to the system log; remove it from release builds
The token is too short; use a longer JWT
The app uses the wrong log level; change I to D
The email address is invalid; validate input
explanation: Logging credentials or tokens is unintended data exposure (OWASP M9). Android's guidance: don't log sensitive information in production.
optionNotes: Correct: logs can be read by tools and other parties with access, so secrets must not be logged.
Length is not the issue; the token should not be logged at all.
Debug level still writes to the log.
The address is fine; the leak is the issue.

stem: An employee receives a text saying a parcel is held and asking her to pay a small fee through a link. Which attack type is this?
options: Phishing delivered by a voice call
Phishing delivered by SMS or messaging apps
Spoofing a Wi-Fi access point name
explanation: Smishing uses text messages with a lure and a link or number. ATT&CK Mobile T1660 Phishing includes SMS and messaging lures; users should report spam texts (7726 in the US).
optionNotes: That is vishing.
Correct: SMS phishing.
That is an evil twin / rogue AP.
That is bluejacking.

stem: Which second factor best resists both SIM swapping and real-time phishing for a high-value account?
options: A FIDO security key or passkey
explanation: CISA: move away from SMS MFA; only FIDO authentication is phishing-resistant. NIST SP 800-63B treats SMS/voice OTP as a restricted authenticator.
optionNotes: Email is weaker still; NIST does not accept it for out-of-band authentication.
SMS codes follow the phone number, which a SIM swap steals.
App codes survive a SIM swap but can still be phished.
Correct: FIDO is bound to the real site and not sent over the phone network.

stem: A traveler wants to charge her phone at an airport kiosk USB port. What is the safest advice?
options: Enable Bluetooth to share the load
Accept the "Trust this computer" prompt so charging is faster
Use her own charger in an AC outlet or a charge-only cable
explanation: Juice jacking abuses public USB ports to load malware or steal data (FCC; ATT&CK Mobile T1458). Power-only charging removes the data path.
optionNotes: USB debugging gives the host even more access.
Bluetooth has nothing to do with charging and adds exposure.
Trusting an unknown host is exactly what juice jacking needs.
Correct: avoids a data connection to an unknown USB host.

stem: What is the purpose of STIR/SHAKEN?
options: Encrypting SMS messages end to end
Authenticating caller ID on calls carried over IP networks to fight spoofing
Detecting SIM swaps at the carrier
explanation: Caller ID spoofing falsifies the displayed number; STIR/SHAKEN is the FCC-backed framework that authenticates it.
optionNotes: SMS is not end-to-end encrypted by STIR/SHAKEN.
Correct: it lets carriers sign and verify caller ID information.
That is Play Protect's role.
SIM swap defenses are carrier PINs and account controls.

stem: A banking app's users report a fake login screen appearing on top of the real app. Which defenses address this attack? (Pick the best combination.)
options: Block the "display over other apps" permission via policy and have the app reject obscured touches
explanation: ATT&CK Mobile T1417.002 GUI Input Capture mimics prompts to steal input. Mitigations: restrict the overlay special permission, user guidance, and app-side tapjacking protections.
optionNotes: Encryption protects data at rest.
Pinning protects traffic, not the screen.
Correct: overlay (GUI input capture) needs the overlay permission; filterTouchesWhenObscured and Android 12+ protections limit it.
Key rotation does not stop another app drawing on screen.

stem: Since Android 9, idle background apps cannot use the camera or microphone. Which technique do spyware apps use to keep sensor access, according to ATT&CK Mobile?
options: Foreground Persistence: running a foreground service with a notification
Rooting the device on every boot
explanation: T1541 Foreground Persistence: apps keep sensor access by running in the foreground. The persistent notification and Android 12+ camera/microphone indicators help users spot it.
optionNotes: Correct: T1541 abuses startForeground() to stay in the foreground.
Rooting is not needed for this and is much harder.
Apps cannot disable SELinux.
INTERNET does not grant sensor access.

stem: EC-Council's "anatomy of a mobile attack" groups the attack surface into three areas. Which set is it?
explanation: EC-Council splits a mobile attack across the device (apps, OS, browser, SMS), the network (Wi-Fi, MITM) and the data center or cloud (servers and databases).
optionNotes: That is an OS architecture view.
Correct: the phone, the connection, and the back end behind the app.
Those are attack phases, not surfaces.
Not the EC-Council grouping.

stem: Since Android 6.0, how are dangerous permissions such as camera or location granted?
options: They are granted by enabling developer options
They are granted silently at install time
Only Google can grant them after review
The app requests them at run time and the user approves a prompt
explanation: Android 6.0 (API 23) introduced runtime permissions: dangerous permissions need an explicit user prompt; special permissions need a Settings toggle.
optionNotes: Developer options do not grant app permissions.
Install-time grant applies to normal (low-risk) permissions.
Google Play review is separate from granting permissions on the device.
Correct: runtime permissions.

stem: Which APK signature scheme introduced signing key rotation?
explanation: v1 JAR signing, v2 whole-APK (7.0), v3 key rotation (9), v4 incremental (11). Sign with all schemes for compatibility.
optionNotes: Correct.
v1 is the original JAR-based signature.
v2 signs the whole file but has no rotation.
v4 supports incremental installation.

stem: A corporate Android phone shows an orange warning screen for ten seconds every time it boots. What does this indicate?
options: The bootloader is unlocked, so the OS may not be verified
The device is enrolled in MDM
explanation: Verified Boot colors: YELLOW locked with custom root of trust, ORANGE unlocked, RED verification failure. An unlocked bootloader is usually the first step to rooting; treat the device as non-compliant.
optionNotes: Hardware health is not shown this way.
Updates don't use the boot warning screens.
Correct: ORANGE is the Verified Boot state for an unlocked device.
MDM enrollment has no boot-screen color.

stem: An app's back end receives a Play Integrity verdict containing only `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY`. What should a sensitive app conclude?
options: The device passed only basic checks; it may be uncertified or have an unlocked bootloader, so limit or deny access
The device is genuine and fully patched
The app was installed from Google Play
explanation: Play Integrity: MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY allows unlocked bootloaders and unverified boot; MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY means a genuine certified device. ATT&CK mitigation M1002 Attestation.
optionNotes: Correct: MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY is missing, so the device is not proven genuine.
That would be MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY.
App origin is in the app verdict (PLAY_RECOGNIZED), not the device verdict.
Integrity verdicts say nothing about user authentication.

stem: An employee installs an app from a link in a text message after turning on "Install unknown apps" for the browser. What is this called, and which control prevents it on managed phones?
options: Sideloading; an MDM policy that blocks installs from unknown sources
explanation: Sideloaded apps skip store vetting. NIST SP 800-124r2 lists restricting sideloading and app stores as an EMM/MAM control; Play Protect scans installed apps.
optionNotes: Jailbreaking is iOS; ATS protects network traffic.
Rooting gains root; installing an APK is not rooting.
Correct: installing outside the official store; MDM can restrict it.
Tethering shares a connection.

stem: A developer needs to store an AES key that encrypts local data on Android. Where should it go?
options: In a file on external storage
In the Android Keystore, hardware-backed where available
explanation: The Android Keystore keeps keys non-extractable and can bind them to secure hardware; StrongBox exists on Android 9+ devices that include it.
optionNotes: External storage is the least protected location.
Other code with access to the app's files could read it.
Hardcoded keys are found by decompiling (OWASP M1/M10).
Correct: key material stays out of the app process and can live in the TEE or StrongBox.

stem: What changed for `android:exported` in apps targeting Android 12 or higher?
options: It now defaults to true for every component
Activities, services and receivers with intent filters must declare it explicitly or the app won't install
It was removed and replaced by permissions
It applies only to content providers
explanation: Android 12 "safer component exporting": declare exported explicitly. Set it to false unless other apps truly need to start the component.
optionNotes: There is no implicit true anymore for these components; the value must be explicit.
Correct: an explicit value is mandatory for components with intent filters.
The attribute still exists.
It applies to activities, services and broadcast receivers.

stem: On a lost-and-found corporate Android phone, an admin plugs in and runs `adb devices`, which returns `List of devices attached 192.168.1.20:5555 device`. What does it show?
options: The phone is enrolled in MDM
The phone is in the boot loader
ADB debugging over TCP port 5555 was enabled on the phone
The phone is connected only by USB with debugging off
explanation: adb tcpip 5555 turns on debugging over the network. Enterprises should disable developer mode and USB debugging by policy (NIST SP 800-124r2).
optionNotes: adb shows nothing about MDM enrollment.
Bootloader mode uses fastboot, not adb devices.
Correct: an IP:5555 entry means network ADB was set up (adb tcpip 5555).
Debugging is clearly on, and over the network.

stem: An app's network security config contains `<base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"><trust-anchors><certificates src="system"/><certificates src="user"/></trust-anchors></base-config>`. What is the risk?
options: It allows plain HTTP and trusts user-installed CAs, easing man-in-the-middle interception
explanation: Secure defaults: no cleartext for apps targeting Android 9+, and apps targeting 7.0+ trust only system CAs. Re-enabling either helps an attacker who installs a CA or sits on the network.
optionNotes: base-config applies to all builds; only debug-overrides is debug-only.
Pinning uses a pin-set; there is none here.
It allows more, not less.
Correct: both settings weaken the secure defaults.

stem: A manifest shows `<application android:allowBackup="true" ...>` in an app that stores medical records. What should the reviewer recommend?
options: Disable backup or exclude sensitive files from it
Nothing, backups are always encrypted end to end
explanation: Android Auto Backup is on by default (up to 25 MB per app). Apps with sensitive data should set allowBackup to false or use backup rules to exclude files.
optionNotes: Correct: allowBackup is true by default; sensitive apps should opt out or exclude data.
Do not assume every backup channel protects the data as the app would.
That adds a new risk.
Unrelated.

stem: Which tool decompiles an APK's DEX bytecode back into readable Java source?
explanation: Reverse engineering tools such as jadx and dex2jar show why secrets must never be hardcoded in an app (OWASP M1, M7).
optionNotes: adb talks to the device; it does not decompile.
Correct: jadx is a DEX-to-Java decompiler.
Nmap scans networks.
Hydra brute-forces logins.

stem: A tester wants to check whether an app's exported activities and content providers can be abused by another app on the same phone. Which tool is built for this?
explanation: drozer assumes the role of an Android app to test the attack surface exposed through IPC (activities, services, receivers, providers).
optionNotes: Correct: drozer acts as an app and interacts with other apps' IPC endpoints.
apktool decodes and rebuilds the package but does not interact with running components.
Burp Suite intercepts HTTP(S) traffic.
Wireshark captures network packets.

stem: Which command-line tool from the Android SDK lists connected devices, opens a shell on them and installs APKs?
explanation: adb has a client, a server and the adbd daemon on the device. Keep USB debugging off on production phones.
optionNotes: apksigner signs and verifies APKs.
Correct: Android Debug Bridge.
jadx decompiles code.
Frida instruments running apps.

stem: How does iOS keep third-party apps from reading each other's files?
options: Each app runs on a separate processor core
All apps share one folder protected by the passcode
Apps are separated only by App Store review
Each app is sandboxed in its own randomly assigned home directory
explanation: All third-party iOS apps are sandboxed; they reach other data only through iOS services and declared entitlements.
optionNotes: CPU cores do not isolate data.
There is no shared folder for all apps.
Review helps, but isolation is enforced on the device.
Correct: sandboxing with a unique container per app.

stem: What is the hardware root of trust in the iPhone secure boot chain?
options: The Boot ROM, which holds the Apple Root CA public key
explanation: Boot ROM → iBoot → kernel: each stage verifies Apple's signature on the next.
optionNotes: The passcode protects data, not the boot chain.
iBoot is the next stage; the Boot ROM verifies it.
Correct: immutable code laid down at chip fabrication.
App signing comes much later, after the kernel runs.

stem: Which iOS Data Protection class applies by default to third-party app data that has no class assigned?
explanation: Class C keys stay available after the first unlock following a reboot. Apps with very sensitive files should choose Complete Protection.
optionNotes: Class B is for files that must be written while locked.
Class A must be chosen explicitly; data becomes unavailable soon after lock.
Correct: Class C is the default.
Class D is only protected by the device UID key.

stem: An iOS app must keep a refresh token between launches. Where should the developer store it?
options: In a plist file inside the app bundle
explanation: Use the Keychain (iOS) or Keystore (Android) for secrets. OWASP M9 and MASVS-STORAGE cover insecure local storage.
optionNotes: UserDefaults is a plain preferences store.
Correct: the Keychain is made for small secrets and has its own protection classes.
Files in the bundle are readable after extraction and are signed, not secret.
The pasteboard can be read by other apps.

stem: A human rights lawyer believes she is targeted by mercenary spyware. Which built-in iPhone feature is designed for her case?
explanation: Apple built Lockdown Mode for the few people personally targeted by sophisticated threats; CISA also recommends it for highly targeted individuals.
optionNotes: Correct: an optional extreme protection that reduces the attack surface.
Screen Time limits usage; it is not an anti-spyware feature.
Low Power Mode saves battery.
Find My locates or erases a lost device.

stem: IT cannot enroll an executive's iPhone in the company MDM: installing the management profile fails. The executive recently enabled a new security option. What is the most likely cause?
options: App Transport Security is blocking the MDM server
Lockdown Mode is on; it blocks configuration profiles and MDM enrollment
explanation: With Lockdown Mode on, configuration profiles can't be installed and the device can't be enrolled in MDM or supervision. It is not an option MDM can set.
optionNotes: Keychain capacity does not affect enrollment.
Supervision makes management easier, not harder.
ATS applies to apps' connections, not profile installation.
Correct: the user must turn Lockdown Mode off, enroll, then turn it back on.

stem: Reviewing an iOS app's Info.plist, you see `NSAppTransportSecurity` → `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true`. What does it do?
options: Turns off App Transport Security, allowing insecure HTTP connections
Allows the app to load code from the internet
explanation: ATS requires TLS 1.2+ with forward secrecy and strong certificates. Global exceptions weaken M5 (Insecure Communication) protection and need justification.
optionNotes: It relaxes security; it does not force a stronger TLS version.
Correct: ATS stops enforcing its requirements for the app's connections.
Pinning is configured separately.
Downloading code is a different (and restricted) behavior.

stem: A game's server wants proof that API requests come from a genuine, unmodified copy of its iOS app, not a script or a tampered build. Which Apple service fits?
explanation: Attestation (App Attest on iOS, Play Integrity on Android) moves trust decisions to the server, which OWASP M7 recommends for important checks.
optionNotes: Correct: it attests that requests come from legitimate instances of the app, with a key in the Secure Enclave.
ATS secures the connection, not the identity of the client app.
Lockdown Mode is a user protection mode.
Data Protection encrypts files at rest.

stem: In EC-Council's terms, which jailbreak lets the device boot normally on its own but loses the jailbreak until it is re-applied from a computer?
explanation: The four EC-Council labels describe what a reboot requires. For defenders, all four mean the same thing: an untrusted device that MDM should block.
optionNotes: Semi-untethered is re-applied from an app on the device, no computer.
Tethered needs the computer to boot at all.
Untethered keeps the jailbreak after reboot.
Correct: boots alone, re-jailbreak needs a computer.

stem: What does COPE stand for in mobile deployment models?
explanation: NIST SP 800-124r2: COPE devices belong to the enterprise, with more lenient restrictions than strict enterprise use; NIST SP 1800-21 is the COPE example solution.
optionNotes: Invented expansion.
Invented expansion.
Correct: the company owns the device and allows some personal use.
Invented expansion.

stem: Employees buy their own phones, but only models from an IT-approved list that can run the company's EMM agent. Which model is this?
explanation: CYOD limits hardware supply-chain risk while keeping personal ownership; NIST notes a BYOD program that rejects devices unable to run the agent is effectively CYOD.
optionNotes: Fully managed devices are company-owned, work use only.
BYOD places no restriction on which personal device is used.
COPE devices are owned by the company.
Correct: Choose Your Own Device.

stem: A stolen company phone is switched off by the thief before IT sends a remote wipe. What does this show?
options: Remote wipe needs power and network, so it must not be the only control
explanation: Combine remote wipe with encryption, a strong passcode and auto-lock, so the data stays protected even if the wipe never arrives.
optionNotes: Native wipe needs the device on and connected.
Correct: NIST calls remote wipe a fundamentally unreliable control on its own.
Nothing suggests a misconfiguration.
Nothing in the scenario says that.

stem: A warehouse uses Android tablets locked to a single inventory app. Which Android Enterprise mode fits?
options: Work profile on a personal device
explanation: Dedicated devices are a subset of company-owned devices locked to a specific purpose; fully managed devices are for company-owned general use.
optionNotes: Correct: company-owned, locked down for one purpose (kiosk).
Work profiles separate work and personal apps; there is no personal use here.
These are not personal devices.
No management at all is the opposite of what is needed.

stem: What is the main difference between MAM and MDM?
options: MAM manages the whole device and MDM only apps
MAM manages enterprise apps without requiring the device to be enrolled
MAM replaces the need for any app vetting
explanation: MAM suits BYOD and partner users: app-level policies, app-level wipe and containers, with less intrusion into personal data.
optionNotes: MAM exists on both platforms.
It is the other way round.
Correct: NIST notes MAM needs no device enrollment or enterprise profile.
Vetting is a separate control.

stem: Security wants rooted or jailbroken phones blocked from corporate email automatically. Which combination does that?
options: EMM compliance policy using device attestation, with conditional access to email
explanation: NIST SP 800-124r2: EMM can limit access by OS version or rooted/jailbroken status. ATT&CK M1002 Attestation: prohibit devices that fail attestation from enterprise resources.
optionNotes: Training helps but enforces nothing.
Wi-Fi passwords don't detect device state.
A VPN encrypts traffic but doesn't check the device.
Correct: detect via attestation/MTD, then block access while non-compliant.

stem: Which Apple enrollment method is designed for BYOD and lets IT manage only the organization's accounts and data?
explanation: Apple: User Enrollment is for devices the user owns; Device Enrollment and ADE give more control for organization-owned devices.
optionNotes: ADE is for organization-owned devices and gives supervision.
Correct: limited payloads, protects personal data.
Supervision is for organization-owned devices.
Lockdown Mode is a user protection mode and blocks enrollment.

stem: A contractor must use a sensitive app, but the company wants no enterprise data stored on the contractor's phone at all. Which NIST-described approach fits?
options: Virtual mobile infrastructure (VMI): the app runs on a hosted virtual phone viewed through a thin client
App wrapping of the contractor's personal apps
Full-device MDM enrollment with full wipe
Sideloading the app from an internal website
explanation: NIST SP 800-124r2: VMI hosts a virtual mobile device and apps in the back end, so sensitive information never sits on the phone (but needs connectivity).
optionNotes: Correct: data stays in the back-end infrastructure.
Wrapping applies policies to apps on the device; data still lands there.
Invasive for a non-employee and data still sits on the device.
Sideloading adds risk and still stores data locally.

stem: In the OWASP MAS project, what is the MASTG?
options: The list of top 10 mobile risks
The testing guide describing how to test mobile apps against MASVS
An Android hardening build of the OS
explanation: MASVS defines the requirements, MASTG the test techniques and tools, MASWE the weaknesses.
optionNotes: MASTG is free documentation, not a product.
That is the OWASP Mobile Top 10.
Correct: Mobile Application Security Testing Guide.
MASTG is not an OS.

stem: Which OWASP MAS profile assumes the device's own user may be the attacker, such as a cheater or reverse engineer?
explanation: MAS-R maps to MASVS-RESILIENCE controls: anti-tampering, anti-debugging, root/jailbreak detection, obfuscation.
optionNotes: L1 is essential security for all apps.
Correct: Resilient security against reverse engineering and tampering.
L2 is advanced security for sensitive apps.
P is baseline privacy.

stem: Which NIST publication describes a process for vetting the security of mobile applications before an organization deploys them?
explanation: SP 800-163r1 (2019) defines app vetting; SP 800-124r2 (2023) covers enterprise mobile device security and references vetting as one technology.
optionNotes: Correct: Vetting the Security of Mobile Applications.
800-124r2 is about managing mobile devices in the enterprise.
800-63B covers authentication.
800-61 covers incident handling.

stem: In MITRE ATT&CK for Mobile, what does mitigation M1002 Attestation recommend?
options: Use remote attestation and block devices that fail it from enterprise resources
explanation: Attestation (Play Integrity, Samsung Knox, App Attest) lets the enterprise or the app back end refuse compromised devices.
optionNotes: That is M1006 Use Recent OS Version.
That is M1011 User Guidance.
That is M1001 Security Updates.
Correct.

stem: A senior official asks for three quick changes to protect her phone accounts from takeover. Which set matches CISA's mobile guidance?
options: Root the phone to install a firewall, use SMS MFA, reuse one strong password
Install a free personal VPN, use SMS MFA, disable updates
Switch to FIDO MFA, disable SMS as a second factor, set a carrier account PIN
Turn off the passcode, use Bluetooth only, avoid Wi-Fi
explanation: CISA's 2025 guidance: E2EE messaging, FIDO, no SMS MFA, password manager, telco PIN, regular updates, latest hardware, no personal VPN.
optionNotes: Rooting removes protections; password reuse is unsafe.
CISA advises against personal VPNs and SMS MFA, and for regular updates.
Correct: phishing-resistant MFA and SIM-swap defenses.
Removing the passcode weakens the device.

stem: A banking app must detect rooted or jailbroken devices, debuggers and repackaging. Which MASVS control group covers this?
explanation: RESILIENCE controls raise the cost of analysis (anti-tampering, anti-debugging, obfuscation); they add to, not replace, the other controls.
optionNotes: PRIVACY covers data minimization and user control.
STORAGE covers sensitive data at rest.
NETWORK covers secure communication.
Correct: resilience against reverse engineering and tampering.

stem: Which dynamic instrumentation toolkit injects JavaScript into a running Android or iOS app to trace and hook its functions?
explanation: Frida injects a JavaScript engine into the target process. Testers use it to verify runtime behavior, such as whether root detection or pinning works.
optionNotes: Correct.
apktool works on the package at rest.
Nessus is a network vulnerability scanner.
Aircrack-ng is a Wi-Fi auditing suite.

stem: Which tool decodes an APK's resources and binary AndroidManifest.xml into readable files and can rebuild the package?
explanation: apktool is a reverse-engineering tool for Android packages; reviewers use it to read the manifest (debuggable, exported, allowBackup).
optionNotes: jadx focuses on decompiling code to Java.
Correct.
adb talks to a device.
objection explores a running app.

stem: A tester sets a phone's Wi-Fi proxy to a laptop and installs the laptop tool's CA certificate to view the app's HTTPS requests. Which tool is this workflow typical of?
explanation: Proxy interception checks OWASP M5. It is also why Android 7+ apps don't trust user-installed CAs by default and why pinning matters.
optionNotes: Nmap scans hosts.
John cracks password hashes.
Correct: Burp Proxy intercepts the app's HTTP(S) traffic.
Metasploit is an exploitation framework.

stem: Which open-source framework produces an automated static analysis report of an APK or IPA, flagging hardcoded secrets and risky manifest settings?
explanation: MobSF performs static and dynamic analysis of Android, iOS and Windows apps; useful in an app vetting pipeline.
optionNotes: Correct: Mobile Security Framework.
Hashcat cracks hashes.
Snort is a network IDS.
Maltego maps OSINT relationships.

stem: Which toolkit, powered by Frida, lets a tester explore an app at run time (file system, keychain, memory) without needing a jailbreak?
explanation: objection supports iOS and Android and is listed in the OWASP MASTG tools. Its findings show why secrets need the Keychain/Keystore and server-side checks.
optionNotes: Androguard analyzes APKs statically.
drozer tests Android IPC endpoints; it is not Frida-based.
dex2jar converts DEX to Java class files.
Correct: runtime mobile exploration built on Frida.
